Learning Objectives
Explain the epidemiology of, etiology of, and risk factors for medial and lateral epicondyle
fractures in pediatric patients.
Perform an appropriate workup for pediatric patients in whom a fracture about the elbow is
suspected.
Review the surgical and nonsurgical management of medial epicondyle fractures in pediatric
patients.

Medial epicondyle fractures can be managed nonsurgically; however, a trend toward surgical
management of medial epicondyle fractures is increasing.1,2
Lateral epicondyle fractures typically are managed nonsurgically unless the fragment is
incarcerated in the elbow joint.1
Epidemiology
Medial Epicondyle Fractures
Age at incidence ranges from 9 to 14 years, with peak incidence among children aged 11 to 12
years.
As many as 50% of these fractures are associated with elbow dislocations, and as many as 15%
to 18% of patients may present with a medial epicondyle incarcerated in the elbow joint.

Medial Epicondyle Fractures
Medial epicondyle fractures account for 14.1% of all distal humerus fractures and 11.5%
of all fractures about the elbow. As many as 50% of medial epicondyle fractures are
associated with elbow dislocations, and as many as 15% to 18% of patients present with
the fragment incarcerated after traumatic fracture-dislocation. The mean age of patients
who sustain medial epicondyle fractures ranges from 9 to 14 years. Most commonly,
children who sustain a medial epicondyle fracture are aged 11 to 12 years. Although
medial epicondyle fractures occur in males and females, these fractures are four times
more common in males.1,3,4
Lateral Epicondyle Fractures
This is a rare injury and not well described in the literature.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
The elbow follows a sequential pattern of ossification and fusion.1


Osteology
The medial epicondyle is the final secondary ossification center to fuse with the distal
humerus. The medial epicondyle arises posterior and medial to the distal humerus, and
it is best appreciated on a lateral radiograph of the elbow (Figure 1; Table 1).
Figure 1 Images show the ossification centers of the distal humerus. A, Illustration
shows the mean time of appearance of ossification centers at the distal humerus. B, AP
radiograph of a right elbow demonstrates the different ossification centers. 1 =
capitellum, 2 = medial epicondyle, 3 = trochlea, 4 = lateral epicondyle. (Reproduced from
Gottschalk HP, Eisner E, Hosalkar HS: Medial epicondyle fractures in the pediatric
population. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2012;20[4]:223-232.)

Vascular Anatomy
Extraosseous: brachial artery within the anterior cubital fossa
Intraosseous—Vascular supply mostly originates from the posterior vascular anastomosis.1
Lateral condyle—Two arteries enter posterior, proximal to the articular cartilage, near the
anconeus origin.
No communication with vessels in the distal humeral metaphysis in skeletally immature
patients.
Trochlea
Lateral ridge (lateral crista) receives blood supply from the vascular supply of the lateral
condyle.
Medial ridge (medial crista) relieves blood supply from vessels that cross the peripheral
physis into the epiphysis.
Medial and lateral epicondyles—Central nutrient vessel of the humeral shaft supplies the
epicondyles.
After physeal closure, metaphyseal and epiphyseal vessels anastamose freely (Figure 2).

Neural Anatomy
Medial Epicondyle

Neural Anatomy
The ulnar nerve passes posterior to the medial epicondyle. The nerve may be pulled into
the joint in circumstances in patients with a traumatic dislocation with incarceration of
the medial epicondyle.3 The median nerve also can become entrapped in the joint if a
dislocated elbow is reduced. A thorough preoperative and postoperative examination,

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004066
5/23

with care taken to document neurovascular abnormalities of all three nerves, is
important in patients before and after closed reduction and/or surgical treatment.
Tendons
Medial Epicondyle
The flexor carpi radialis, the flexor carpi ulnaris, the flexor digitorum superficialis, the palmaris
longus, and a portion of the pronator teres originate from the anterior aspect of the medical
epicondyle via the common flexor tendon.
A portion of the flexor carpi ulnaris also originates from the posterior portion of the medial
epicondyle.
Lateral Epicondyle
The common extensor muscles originate from the lateral epicondyle.
Joints and Ligaments
Medial Epicondyle
Anterior and posterior bands of the ulnar collateral ligament arise from the medial epicondyle.
Anterior band provides stability against valgus force with the elbow in extension.5-7
Posterior band provides stability with the elbow is in flexion (Figure 3).

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Medial Epicondyle Fractures
Most common mechanism is an avulsion injury.
Fractures resulting from a direct blow have been described but are less common.

Medial Epicondyle Fractures
Fractures may be caused by avulsion injuries if the patient falls onto an outstretched
extremity with the elbow extended. At the time of impact, the valgus force across the
elbow may result an avulsion fracture of the medical epicondyle in a patient with a
tension-type injury. Associated injuries with this mechanism include radial neck and
olecranon fractures. Sudden avulsion injuries also may occur with rapid flexor
contraction, such as in throwing or arm wrestling. Rarely, a direct blow to the posterior
medial elbow may result in a medial epicondyle fracture. These fractures may appear
comminuted and minimally displaced.1,3
Lateral Epicondyle Fractures
A direct blow is the most common mechanism of injury.

Lateral Epicondyle Fractures
The most common etiology is a direct blow to the lateral elbow; however, avulsion
fractures associated with avulsion of the common extensor muscles and the extensor
carpi radialis longus also have been described.
SEND FEEDBACK

Risk Factors
Medial epicondyle fractures may be related to repetitive stress injury.
No well-described risk factors for lateral epicondyle fractures have been described.

Risk Factors
Medial epicondyle fractures may result from chronic stress/repetitive tension injuries,
such as in youth baseball players and other throwing athletes. These patients may have
a history of repetitive medial elbow pain after throwing before sustaining a fracture.8
Associated Injuries
Approximately 50% of medial epicondyle fractures are associated with elbow dislocations.1,4
Injury Classification
Medial epicondyle fracture classification1
Nondisplaced or minimally displaced injuries
Displaced fractures
Incarcerated fractures
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History

Patient History
A thorough patient history should include the mechanism of the injury, any antecedent
pain, and any subjective paresthesias or difficulty with finger/wrist range of motion since
the time of injury. Apophysitis of the medial epicondyle, or Little Leaguer’s elbow, is
common in throwers and may precede fracture. The examiner also should ask about the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:41 PM
AAOS | Medial Epicondyle and Lateral Epicondyle Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004066
8/23

patient’s daily activities, including the type of sports the patient participates in and the
level at which they participate.3
Physical Examination
Valgus stress test, with or without fluoroscopy, to evaluate for instability in the elbow

Physical Examination
Visual inspection of the elbow is an important aspect of the physical examination.
Patterns of bruising may be indicative of the underlying fracture pattern. Typically,
patients with a medial epicondyle fracture have swelling and bruising posteromedial to
the elbow, whereas patients with a lateral epicondyle fracture have focal ecchymosis
laterally. Substantial global swelling and ecchymoses may be indicative of an elbow
dislocation with spontaneous reduction. Patients also should be evaluated for
underlying elbow effusion. This may be indicative of an associated dislocation or other
intra-articular injury. An isolated medial or lateral epicondyle avulsion fracture typically is
not associated with a large hemarthrosis. A valgus stress test, with or without
fluoroscopy, can be performed to evaluate for instability in patients with a medial
epicondyle fracture; however, the examination likely will be limited because of pain and
apprehension.3,9 The test should be performed with the patient in the supine position,
with the shoulder abducted and externally rotated approximately 90°. The elbow also
should be slightly flexed to eliminate the stabilizing force of the olecranon during the
test.
Neurovascular Examination
With medial epicondyle fractures, documenting nerve function is critical.
Anterior transposition of the ulnar nerve may occur with these injuries.
Incarceration of the nerve and the medial epicondyle fragment in the elbow joint is possible,
and patients may present with ulnar nerve neuropraxia.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:41 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004066
9/23

The median nerve also may become entrapped if a dislocated elbow is reduced. Therefore, a
thorough neurologic examination before and after reduction is important in patients with an
elbow dislocation.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Standard AP, lateral, and oblique views may under-represent the degree of fracture
displacement, particularly for medial epicondyle fractures (Figure 4).
Edmonds10 recommended obtaining a flexed elbow view to measure the true degree of
medial epicondyle fracture displacement.

Radiography
A true lateral radiograph of the elbow is critical, particularly after a medial epicondyle
fracture with a known elbow dislocation, to evaluate for a possible incarcerated medial
epicondyle fragment (Figure 5). The articulation between the distal humerus and the
proximal ulna should be symmetric and uniform on lateral, AP, and oblique views.
Widening of this articulation, particularly if the medial epicondyle fragment is not visible
on a lateral radiograph, should increase suspicion for an incarcerated fragment.1,3
Standard radiographs may underestimate the amount of fracture displacement;
therefore, a flexed elbow view or other more advanced imaging studies, such as CT
scans, MRIs, or ultrasonographic images, can be obtained to better evaluate the degree
of fracture displacement or identify an unossified epicondyle, if necessary.10,11
Computed Tomography
CT may demonstrate the degree of displacement of the fracture fragment better than plain
radiographs, especially the degree of anterior displacement.
However, routine CT generally is recommended for these injuries and is best reserved for
cases in which the practitioner is trying to decide between surgical and nonsurgical
management.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI also is not routinely recommended but may be considered if concern exists for other
chondral or ligamentous injury or an incarcerated unossified epicondyle that may not be
appreciated on plain radiographs.

Differential Diagnosis
Medial Epicondyle Fractures
Elbow dislocation with an associated medial epicondyle fracture
Medial condyle fracture

Differential Diagnosis
The main differential diagnosis, in addition to an elbow dislocation with an associated
medial epicondyle fracture, is a medial condyle fracture.1 A large hemarthrosis and/or a
large associated metaphyseal fracture fragment with the medial epicondyle should
increase suspicion for a medial condyle fracture. In this circumstance, additional imaging
via CT, MRI, or arthrography aids in distinguishing these injuries.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Medial Epicondyle Fractures
Indications
Nonsurgical management has been the mainstay of treatment for fractures with less than 5
mm of displacement.12
Contraindications
Incarcerated fragments in the elbow joint and open fractures are absolute indications for
surgical management.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:41 PM
AAOS | Medial Epicondyle and Lateral Epicondyle Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004066
12/23

Techniques
Closed attempts to extricate an entrapped medial condyle may be undertaken by supinating
the forearm, placing a valgus stress on the elbow, and extending the wrist and fingers.1
Early motion (within 3 to 5 days) minimizes the risk of elbow stiffness.13-15
Outcomes
Outcomes of nonsurgical management of medial epicondyle fractures generally are good.

Outcomes
Farsetti et al16 reported on a minimum 30-year follow-up of medial epicondyle fractures,
comparing nonsurgical management with surgical fixation or fracture fragment excision.
Patients who underwent nonsurgical treatment had outcomes identical to those of
patients who underwent surgical stabilization with regard to function, range of motion,
and pain, despite having a substantially higher rate of fracture nonunion. Patients who
underwent fracture excision had universally poor outcomes; however, contemporary
multisport pediatric athletes may have increased demands on their elbows compared
with this cohort from Italy in 1950 through 1980. Lawrence et al17 compared the
outcomes of throwing athletes who sustained a medial epicondyle fracture and were
treated surgically or nonsurgically. No differences were observed between the groups
with regard to range of motion, stability (subjective or objective), or return to sport.
However, this study was not a randomized controlled trial, all elbow dislocations were
managed surgically, and mean fracture displacement was greater in the patients treated
surgically.
Tadlock et al18 performed a systematic review of pediatric athletes, comparing the
outcomes of surgical versus nonsurgical management of medial epicondyle fractures.
Patients treated nonsurgically experienced lower complication rates and equivalent
functional outcomes; therefore, the authors concluded that nonsurgical treatment may
be a valid treatment option for athletes. In patients treated surgically, Patel et al
reported excellent outcomes at a mean follow-up of 6.3 years; however, 41% of the

patients required hardware removal. Screw fixation has been shown to be the strongest
and stiffest construct compared with Kirschner wires or suture anchors.19,20
Although trends toward surgical fixation of medial epicondyle fractures are increasing,
the current literature does not demonstrate a consistently superior outcome in
surgically treated patients compared with nonsurgically treated patients; however, all
studies are associated with selection bias.21,22
Lateral Epicondyle Fractures
Nonsurgical management is indicated for most lateral epicondyle fractures. Surgical
management is indicated if the epicondyle has displaced into the elbow joint.1
Surgical Management
Indications
Medial epicondyle fractures
Absolute: intra-articular entrapment of the medial epicondyle and open fractures
Relative: fracture of the dominant arm in a throwing athlete or a weight-bearing extremity in
an athlete (such as a gymnast), fracture associated with elbow dislocation, displacement more
5 mm (controversial), and ulnar nerve dysfunction
Lateral epicondyle fractures
Absolute: intra-articular entrapment of the lateral epicondyle
Most fractures are managed nonsurgically.
Techniques/Procedures for Medial Epicondyle Fractures
Technique—Open reduction with screw fixation is preferred to allow for early motion.
Kirschner wires may be used in young children.
Patient Positioning

Patients can be placed in the supine or prone position. A recent study did not report any
differences in the length of the surgical procedure performed via the supine or prone position.
Prone patient positioning required additional setup time.23
In patients in the supine position, the forearm must be pronated and the wrist must flexed to
take tendon off the common flexor origin to allow for appropriate fracture reduction.
In patients in the prone position, the shoulder and elbow are flexed approximately 90° on an
arm board, and the forearm naturally rests in pronation, which may aid in relaxation of the
common flexor origin and fracture reduction.24,25 (Figures 6 and 7).
Figure 6 Intraoperative photograph shows patient positioning for open reduction and fixation of
a medial epicondyle fracture. A hand table is attached to the surgical side, and the arm is allowed
to rest in a flexed pronated position with the shoulder internally rotated. The patient must have
adequate internal rotation of the shoulder. (Reproduced with permission from Glotzbecker MP,
Shore B, Matheney T, Gold M, Hedequist D: Alternative technique for open reduction and fixation
of displaced pediatric medial epicondyle fractures. J Child Orthop 2012;6[2]:105-109.)

Surgical Approaches
A 2- to 4-cm incision is made over the posteromedial aspect of the elbow directly over the
origin of the medial epicondyle.
A longer incision may be helpful if dissection of the ulnar nerve is required. This may be most
helpful if the medial epicondyle is incarcerated within the elbow because, in these
circumstances, the ulnar nerve may be displaced anteriorly and may need to be carefully
dissected to retract it posteriorly without applying excessive tension to the nerve.
Surgical Fracture Fixation
A towel clip can be used to hold the fragment in the reduced position until the fragment is
stabilized with the use of a Kirschner wire and a derotational Kirschner wire. In younger
patients, a towel clip can be placed on the flexor-pronator mass to avoid fragmenting the
already small epicondyle. A 3.5-mm or 4.0-mm screw, with or without a washer, can then be
placed to definitively stabilize the fracture (Figure 8).
In younger children or patients in whom a screw cannot be placed, such as those with fracture
comminution, alternative methods of fixation, such as Kirschner wires or suture anchors, can
be used to stabilize the fragment.

Postoperative Management
The main advantage of surgical fixation, particularly if rigid internal fixation (screw) is used, is
early joint mobilization. Therefore, the elbow generally is immobilized in a splint or a cast for 1
to 2 weeks postoperatively, after which patients are transitioned to an active range of motion
program.
Contact sports, throwing, and lifting are contraindicated until fracture healing is observed.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Failure to adequately relax the flexor-pronator mass may make reduction of the medial
epicondyle to its origin difficult. In some patients who undergo delayed treatment,
musculotendinous lengthening of the flexor-pronator mass proximally may be necessary to
facilitate anatomic reduction.
Failure to identify malpositioning intraoperatively will lead to malunion.
Complications
Nonunion
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:41 PM
AAOS | Medial Epicondyle and Lateral Epicondyle Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004066
17/23

Medial Epicondyle Fractures
This incidence of nonunion is higher in fractures managed nonsurgically; however, nonunion
does not necessarily correlate with poorer functional outcomes or symptomatic elbow
instability.
The incidence of nonunion is low in fractures managed surgically.
Larger, prospective, comparative studies of patients with a medial epicondyle fracture
managed surgically and versus nonsurgically are necessary to determine the true incidence of
symptomatic nonunion among patients treated nonsurgically.4,16,17
Lateral Epicondyle Fractures
Nonunion can occur but seldom is symptomatic.
Malunion
Medial Epicondyle Fractures

Medial Epicondyle Fractures
The incidence of nonunion or malunion is higher in patients who are treated
nonsurgically; however, the incidence of symptomatic malunion is not well known, and
additional studies are necessary.4 Malunion among surgically treated patients results
from failure to restore the medial epicondyle to its origin. Optimizing patient positioning
to relax the flexor-pronator mass is key to reduce the medial epicondyle to its origin. A
critical review of the reduction, particularly on intraoperative lateral fluoroscopic images
of the elbow, also helps prevent malreduction. If necessary, a lateral image of the
contralateral elbow can be obtained preoperatively for use as a reference
intraoperatively.
Hardware Malpositioning
Medial Epicondyle Fractures

Medial Epicondyle Fractures
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:41 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004066
18/23

The trajectory of the screw is slightly medial to lateral on an AP view and posterior to
anterior on a lateral view. A screw trajectory that is too lateral may result in a portion of
the screw terminating within the coronoid or the olecranon fossa, leading to
impingement in terminal flexion or extension. A screw directed too anteriorly may be
prominent anteriorly. Screws typically are placed just short of the lateral cortex to avoid
cortical penetration leading to possible injury to the radial nerve.
Stiffness

Stiffness
Stiffness is almost universal but rarely of functional consequence. Patients may lose 5%
to 10% of terminal extension but infrequently are symptomatic. This is true regardless of
mangaement.1 Shorter periods of immobilization have been associated with improved
overall range of motion.14
Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
Ulnar neuropathy generally is a neurapraxia, which spontaneously resolves.
Other Complications
Chronic instability is rare but may occur in patients with a fracture associated with an elbow
dislocation.
Failed diagnosis of an incarcerated medial epicondyle may lead to elbow stiffness and
degenerative changes.26
Prominent, symptomatic hardware may necessitate return to the operating room for
hardware removal.
Rehabilitation
Medial Epicondyle Fractures
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:41 PM
AAOS | Medial Epicondyle and Lateral Epicondyle Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004066
19/23

Short-term immobilization followed by an active range of motion program to prevent stiffness
is key.
High-impact activities, such as throwing and gymnastics, are discouraged for at least 6 to 8
weeks postoperatively.
Outcomes
Medial Epicondyle Fractures
Outcomes generally are good, regardless of management.
Early mobilization to prevent stiffness is key to regaining range of motion, regardless whether
patients are treated surgically or nonsurgically.12,18,19
Lateral Epicondyle Fractures
Outcomes are good.
The only major complication is a missed incarcerated fragment in the elbow joint.
